title: Charleston County begins 2026-27 AI-literacy rollout for teachers and students
subtitle: The South Carolina district is one of the first in the US to pair in-person and online AI training across educators and secondary students in a single year.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Charleston County School District in South Carolina has launched its 2026-27 AI-literacy rollout, offering combined online and in-person training to educators and to middle- and high-school students in a single academic year. The district is one of the first large US systems to move past isolated pilots and run a parallel teacher-and-student program, pairing a professional-development track for staff with a classroom curriculum that students work through alongside their teachers rather than independently.

The structural choice is deliberate. Many district pilots have trained teachers first and asked them to filter the curriculum down to students in a second year — which, in practice, often meant students were using AI tools informally for a full year before any formal instruction. Charleston's model collapses the timeline: the professional-development sessions and the student units run on the same calendar, so the first time a student uses an AI tool in school is also when a trained teacher is in the room. The district is covering foundational literacy (what an LLM is, where its outputs come from), evaluation (recognizing hallucinations and citations), and ethics (academic integrity, bias, data privacy).

Charleston's rollout joins a widening list — Boston Public Schools made AI fluency a graduation requirement for high schoolers starting September 2026, Philadelphia's 'Pioneering AI in School Systems' trains administrators, principals, and teachers in role-specific tracks, and Illinois issued statewide guidance earlier this year. The pattern is converging on a two-year arc: the 2024-25 and 2025-26 cycles were about policy and pilots; 2026-27 is where the training actually hits classrooms at scale. The variable now is not whether districts will train — it's whether the curriculum keeps pace with how fast the tools underneath it change.

A takeaway for learners: if you teach, or you're training to teach, the open question in AI literacy right now is content durability. A unit built around a specific tool goes stale in a semester; a unit built around a transferable skill — 'read this output and tell me which claim you'd verify first' — survives model upgrades. The best districts right now are quietly rewriting their curricula every six months. If you want a template, Charleston's public documentation and Illinois's statewide guidance from July are two of the clearest free references available.
